data.sourcePassage:
The Great Plague of 1665 was one of the last major outbreaks of bubonic plague in England. At its worst point, around 100,000 people may have died in London, though exact figures are debated because record-keeping was imperfect. Modern scientists understand the disease as a bacterial infection — Yersinia pestis — spread by fleas carried on rats. But Londoners in 1665 did not know this. They saw sudden illness, painful swellings called buboes, fever, weakness, and death. They tried to explain what was happening using the knowledge they had: some believed plague was God's punishment for sin, others blamed bad air (miasma), and others still looked to astrology.

Several factors helped plague spread rapidly in London. The city was crowded with narrow streets, cramped housing, and inadequate waste disposal, creating perfect conditions for rats and fleas. Wealthier Londoners could sometimes leave for the countryside, but poorer families were less likely to be able to move. The government issued plague orders: infected houses were locked and marked with a red cross, watchmen prevented residents from leaving, streets were cleaned, and some public gatherings were closed. Bills of Mortality — weekly death records — were published to track the epidemic's progress.

Some of these measures helped a little. Separating infected households reduced contact, and recording deaths gave authorities useful information. But other actions were counterproductive. Killing cats and dogs — mistakenly blamed for spreading disease — may have reduced predators that hunted rats. Shutting up infected houses was especially harsh: healthy family members could be locked in with sick relatives for weeks, and some families hid symptoms to avoid being sealed in. The plague reveals much about early modern society: the limits of medical knowledge, the power of religion, and the unequal burden on the poor.

questions.question: What was the name given to the belief that disease was caused by bad air?
options: Germ theory
Quarantine
Miasma
Humourism

questions.question: Why did shutting up infected houses sometimes make things worse?
options: Because it prevented doctors from reaching patients
Because healthy family members could be locked in with sick relatives, and families hid symptoms to avoid being sealed in
Because it stopped the Bills of Mortality from being published
Because it prevented people from going to church
questions.modelAnswer: Shutting up infected houses sometimes made things worse because healthy family members could be locked inside with sick relatives for weeks. Some families chose to hide symptoms to avoid being sealed in, which meant infected people continued to move around and spread the disease.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the relationship between historical understanding and modern knowledge when studying the plague?
options: Modern historians should dismiss early modern explanations as simply wrong
Early modern Londoners were stupid for not knowing about bacteria
We should understand why early modern explanations seemed sensible given what people knew, while also using modern science to understand what was actually happening
Only modern scientific explanations are relevant to studying history
questions.modelAnswer: The passage suggests historians should do both: understand why early modern explanations made sense to people at the time (they had no concept of bacteria, and religious and environmental explanations fitted their worldview), while also using modern scientific knowledge to understand the actual mechanisms of disease spread. Dismissing past people as stupid prevents genuine historical understanding.

data.sourcePassage:
In the early hours of 2 September 1666, a fire broke out in a bakery in Pudding Lane, owned by a baker named Thomas Farriner. The fire quickly spread through the old City of London, burning for four days. When it was finally brought under control, an estimated 13,000 houses had been destroyed, along with around 87 parish churches and old St Paul's Cathedral. Hundreds of thousands of people were left homeless.

The fire spread so rapidly for multiple reasons that historians must consider together. London's buildings were mostly timber-framed, with upper floors projecting out over narrow streets, so flames could jump easily from building to building. That summer had been dry, making the wood tinder-dry. Strong east winds pushed the fire westward through the City. Riverside warehouses were packed with flammable goods including tar, pitch, and oil. Firefighting efforts were delayed by poor early decisions — the Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, was famously criticised for dismissing the early fire as insignificant. When firebreaks were eventually ordered, building owners resisted having their properties demolished unless absolutely necessary.

Despite enormous destruction, recorded deaths from the fire were surprisingly low. However, this does not mean the human cost was small. Thousands lost their homes, businesses, goods, and records. Some notable consequences followed: new building regulations required more brick and stone, some streets were widened, Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral and fifty other churches, and the concept of fire insurance developed more quickly. The Great Fire did not, as is sometimes claimed, end the plague — that epidemic had already largely subsided before the fire. But the rebuilding of London that followed eventually created a somewhat safer city.

The plague was in decline for its own reasons. The Fire therefore cannot have 'cured' a disease that was already largely gone.

data.sourceTitle: The Scientific Revolution and Witch Trials
data.targetTitle: The Scientific Revolution and Witch Trials
data.sourcePassage:
The seventeenth century is often described as a time of scientific revolution. In England, the Royal Society was founded in 1660, bringing together natural philosophers who wanted to promote observation, experiment, and shared evidence. Their motto 'Nullius in verba' — roughly 'take nobody's word for it' — challenged the older practice of simply accepting the authority of ancient writers. Members like Robert Hooke and Robert Boyle used instruments such as microscopes and air pumps to investigate nature. This represented a significant change from earlier approaches to knowledge.

Yet this revolution in thinking was not complete or universal. Many educated people continued to use older explanations alongside newer ones. Miasma remained widely believed. Religious explanations for disaster continued to carry great weight. Astrology was still practised. The same century that saw the Royal Society founded also saw some of the most intense witch-hunting in English history. Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled 'Witchfinder General', was responsible for the deaths of perhaps 300 people in East Anglia between 1645 and 1647. His activities took place during the chaos and fear of the English Civil War, when normal authority had broken down.

Witchcraft accusations were not simply the result of ignorance. They grew from genuine fears about evil and the Devil, from local quarrels and resentments, from gender inequality (most accused were older or poorer women), from the social strain of poverty, and from the weakness of evidence standards. As courts gradually became more sceptical about witch-mark evidence and confessions obtained through pressure, prosecutions declined. Witchcraft laws were finally repealed in 1736. Historians remind us that understanding the witch trials requires us to understand the social, religious, and legal world of early modern England — not simply dismiss the past as superstitious.

questions.question: According to the passage, what does it mean to say the Scientific Revolution was 'not complete or universal'?
options: The Royal Society failed to do any useful experiments
Only farmers and working people kept older beliefs
Even educated people continued using older explanations like miasma and astrology alongside newer scientific methods
Science only changed things in France, not England
questions.modelAnswer: Saying the Scientific Revolution was 'not complete or universal' means that even as new experimental approaches became more influential, many educated people continued to use older explanations — miasma, astrology, religious explanations — at the same time. The change was gradual and uneven, not a sudden replacement of all old ideas.

questions.question: According to the passage, what were the social causes that made witchcraft accusations happen?
options: Witchcraft accusations were purely random and unpredictable
Only uneducated people made accusations, and the educated never believed in witches
Accusations grew from fear of the Devil, local quarrels, gender inequality, poverty, and weak evidence standards
All accusations were organised by the government to control the population
questions.modelAnswer: The passage identifies several social causes: genuine religious fears about the Devil, local quarrels and resentments, gender inequality (most accused were older or poorer women), the social strain of poverty, and the weakness of evidence standards that allowed rumour and dubious 'witch marks' to be used as proof. Understanding these social contexts is essential to understanding why accusations happened.
